theme: O LORD, God of my salvation, the darkest lament
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 88. It is the darkest psalm in the Psalter, and it is meant to be. Read it slowly and do not hurry to a happy ending. There is not one. Notice how it begins, and notice what the psalmist keeps doing.
settingTheScene: Psalm 88 is attributed to Heman the Ezrahite, a wise man mentioned in 1 Kings 4:31. It is the only lament in the Psalter that ends with no note of hope. Other laments move from complaint to trust. This one begins in darkness and ends in darkness. Why would the Bible include a prayer like this? The answer is that God knows some of his people will walk through seasons that feel exactly like it, and he wants them to know that they are allowed to pray in that darkness. Compare it to Job in his worst chapters.
observation: The first line is a statement of faith: “O LORD, God of my salvation” (v. 1).
He cries “day and night” before God and asks that his prayer would come before him (vv. 1-2).
“My soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol” (v. 3). He feels like one who is already dead (vv. 4-5).
“You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep” (v. 6).
“Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves” (v. 7).
“You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them” (v. 8).
“Every day I call upon you, O LORD; I spread out my hands to you” (v. 9).
He asks, “Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you?” (v. 10).
“But I, O LORD, cry to you; in the morning my prayer comes before you” (v. 13).
“O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?” (v. 14).
The last line is “my companions have become darkness” (v. 18).
interpretation:
Start with what the psalm does not have. There is no turn. No “But you.” No vow to praise. No assurance that God has heard. The psalmist ends with the word “darkness.” If you came to this psalm hoping to be cheered up, you will be disappointed.

But look at what the psalm does have. It begins with “O LORD, God of my salvation.” This is the only line in the psalm that points to light, and it comes first. Whatever else is true, the psalmist is still talking to the God who saves. He does not understand how God can be his salvation and feel like his enemy. But he refuses to stop addressing him. And he says, “Every day I call upon you.” He keeps praying. He spreads out his hands. In verse 13, he says that his prayer will come before God “in the morning.” The darkness has not stopped him from praying.

That is the quiet wonder of the psalm. Faith in this psalm is not a feeling of hope. It is the act of continuing to pray when there is no feeling. It is clinging to the one who seems to be against you. The psalm itself is a prayer, and so it is itself the evidence that the psalmist has not let go.

It is also important to see that God’s word includes this prayer. The Bible does not demand that all faith be cheerful. It gives a place for the person who has no light, and it says, in effect, “Here are words you can use.” If you ever find yourself unable to say anything hopeful, this psalm says that you can still say, “LORD, God of my salvation,” and keep praying.

Finally, the psalm points to Christ. The one who, more than any other, was shunned by companions and overwhelmed by waves of wrath is Jesus. On the cross he took the wrath that lay heavy on us, and he went into the darkness so that we could come out of it. Psalm 88 is, in a deeper sense, his prayer.
connection: Jesus’ experience of being deserted by his friends (Mark 14:50) and of bearing the wrath of God is a fulfillment of this psalm. Lamentations 3:1-18 is another prayer that ends in the dark, until verse 19 and following. Hebrews 5:7 describes Jesus offering up prayers with loud cries and tears. Romans 8:26 says the Spirit prays for us when we cannot.
application:
If you are in a dark season, pray this psalm. You do not need to add a happy ending. Say “LORD, God of my salvation,” and then say whatever is true.

If you know someone who is in a dark season, resist the urge to hand them a quick answer. Sit with them. Sometimes the best thing you can do is to pray Psalm 88 with them.

Thank Jesus for going into the darkness for you, and for the promise that one day there will be no more.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what the dark feels like, without tidying it up.
Thank Jesus for going into the dark for you.
Hold in prayer someone you love who is in the dark today.
